author: A Robot
objectives: Determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral).
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry, identifying the shape produced when one or more domains is a lone pair.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs and predict bond-angle deviations from idealized values.
Apply VSEPR predictions to specific molecules and compare predicted geometries to experimentally observed structures.

modules.description: Introduces the central idea of VSEPR theory: electron domains around a central atom repel each other and arrange to minimize repulsion. Reviews how to count electron domains from a Lewis structure.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: State the core principle of VSEPR theory (electron domain repulsion minimization).
Count electron domains (bonding pairs and lone pairs) from a Lewis structure.
instructions: Watch the central atom and reference panel as the narrator introduces VSEPR theory.

clips.changeMeaning: The central atom appears alone in the workspace to orient students before any electron domains are introduced.
clips.narration: Welcome to VSEPR theory. Molecules aren't flat, even though we often draw them that way. VSEPR theory - Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion - lets us predict the true three-dimensional shape of a molecule starting from its Lewis structure. The core idea is simple: electron pairs around a central atom repel each other, and the molecule adopts whatever arrangement pushes these electron domains as far apart as possible.

clips.changeMeaning: The reference Lewis structure panel for water fades in beside the central atom to demonstrate domain counting from a familiar flat diagram.
clips.narration: Let's review how to count electron domains. Here is water, drawn as a flat Lewis structure. Each single bond, double bond, triple bond, or lone pair around the central atom counts as exactly one electron domain, regardless of whether it's a single, double, or triple bond. Oxygen here has two bonding domains and two lone pair domains - four domains total.

clips.changeMeaning: No object changes; this clip closes the introduction and verbally bridges to the next module's live repulsion demonstration.
clips.narration: VSEPR theory takes this flat, two-dimensional Lewis structure as input, and predicts the real three-dimensional shape the molecule actually adopts. In the next scene, we'll watch electron domains repel each other in real time and settle into their minimum-repulsion arrangement.

modules.moduleName: Minimum Repulsion: Building the Electron-Domain Geometries
modules.description: Demonstrates the minimum-repulsion principle directly by showing electron domain clouds repel and settle into linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral arrangements as domains are added one at a time.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Observe how electron domains repel and settle into minimum-repulsion configurations.
Identify the linear (2 domains, 180°), trigonal planar (3 domains, 120°), and tetrahedral (4 domains, 109.5°) electron-domain geometries.
instructions: Watch as electron domains are added one by one and observe how they rearrange.

clips.changeMeaning: Two electron domain clouds appear at arbitrary, non-ideal starting positions around the central atom to set up the repulsion animation.
clips.narration: Let's start with two electron domains around a central atom, placed at arbitrary starting positions. Watch what happens as they repel one another.

clips.changeMeaning: The two domains move to their final linear, 180-degree-apart positions, demonstrating the settled minimum-repulsion configuration, and the label updates.
clips.narration: The two domains drift apart, repelled by one another, until they settle exactly 180 degrees apart. This is the linear electron-domain geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: A third domain cloud is introduced and all three domains reposition into the trigonal planar arrangement at 120 degrees, illustrating the geometry change with an added domain.
clips.narration: Now let's add a third domain. Watch all three rearrange themselves into a new minimum-repulsion configuration: trigonal planar, with domains spaced 120 degrees apart.

clips.changeMeaning: A fourth domain cloud is added and the whole set rearranges into a three-dimensional tetrahedral configuration at 109.5 degrees, completing the domain-addition sequence for this scene.
clips.narration: A fourth domain joins the group. The flat arrangement can no longer minimize repulsion, so the domains pop out into three dimensions, forming a tetrahedron with angles of 109.5 degrees.

modules.moduleName: Completing the Geometry Catalog: 5 and 6 Domains
modules.description: Extends the tetrahedron to five and six domains, forming trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral geometries, culminating in a side-by-side summary of all five electron-domain geometries.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the trigonal bipyramidal geometry (5 domains: 3 equatorial at 120°, 2 axial at 90°).
Identify the octahedral geometry (6 domains, all neighbors at 90°).
Recall all five electron-domain geometries with their domain counts and characteristic angles.
instructions: Rotate the molecule to inspect the geometry from any angle.
Review the final summary panel comparing all five geometries.

clips.changeMeaning: Three equatorial domains settle into the trigonal planar base while two axial domains appear above and below, forming the trigonal bipyramidal geometry for five total domains.
clips.narration: Starting from our tetrahedron, let's add a fifth electron domain. Watch the geometry rearrange into a trigonal bipyramid: three equatorial domains at 120 degrees to each other, and two axial domains at 90 degrees to the equatorial plane.

clips.changeMeaning: A conceptual sixth domain position is introduced by repositioning the equatorial domains into a symmetric octahedral arrangement with the axial domains, and the label updates to reflect octahedral geometry.
clips.narration: Now a sixth domain joins. The two axial positions become equivalent to the equatorial ones, and everything reorganizes into an octahedron - six domains, every neighboring angle exactly 90 degrees. Feel free to rotate the molecule and inspect it from any angle.

clips.changeMeaning: A summary panel fades in showing all five electron-domain geometries side by side with their domain counts and angles, consolidating the module's content.
clips.narration: Here is a summary of all five electron-domain geometries: linear with 2 domains at 180 degrees, trigonal planar with 3 domains at 120 degrees, tetrahedral with 4 domains at 109.5 degrees, trigonal bipyramidal with 5 domains at 90 and 120 degrees, and octahedral with 6 domains all at 90 degrees.

modules.description: Uses the tetrahedral arrangement to show how replacing bonded atoms with lone pairs changes the molecular geometry (methane to ammonia to water) while the electron-domain geometry stays tetrahedral.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry.
Identify trigonal pyramidal and bent molecular geometries as lone-pair modifications of tetrahedral electron-domain geometry.
instructions: Observe how the molecular shape changes as lone pairs replace bonded atoms.

clips.changeMeaning: Methane's four bonded hydrogens are shown around the central carbon in tetrahedral positions, establishing the baseline case where electron-domain and molecular geometry match.
clips.narration: Here is methane, CH4. Four bonding domains extend from carbon to four hydrogen atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement. Since every domain is a bonding pair, the electron-domain geometry and the molecular geometry are identical: both tetrahedral.

components.text:
Ammonia (NH3)
Electron-Domain: Tetrahedral
Molecular: Trigonal Pyramidal

clips.changeMeaning: One hydrogen atom is removed and replaced by a translucent lone-pair cloud in the same tetrahedral position, transforming methane into ammonia and changing the molecular geometry label while the electron-domain geometry stays the same.
clips.narration: Now watch what happens when we replace one hydrogen with a lone pair. This is ammonia, NH3. The electron-domain geometry is still tetrahedral - four domains, same arrangement - but the molecular geometry, the shape traced by the atoms alone, is now trigonal pyramidal.

clips.changeMeaning: A second hydrogen is removed and replaced with a lone-pair cloud, transforming ammonia into water and updating the label to show the molecular geometry is now bent while electron-domain geometry remains tetrahedral.
clips.narration: Now a second hydrogen is replaced with a lone pair. This is water, H2O. The electron-domain geometry has remained tetrahedral throughout this entire sequence, but the molecular geometry is now bent. Lone pairs are not 'seen' as part of the molecular shape, even though they still occupy space and influence the geometry.

modules.description: Compares methane, ammonia, and water side by side to show how lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, compressing bond angles from 109.5° to 107° to 104.5°.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs.
Predict the direction of bond-angle compression as lone pairs replace bonding pairs (109.5° → 107° → 104.5°).
instructions: Compare the three molecules and their labeled bond angles.
Toggle the overlay view to see how the bonding angle shrinks as lone pairs are added.

clips.changeMeaning: All three reference molecules with their bond angle labels are displayed together for direct visual comparison of decreasing bond angles as lone pairs increase.
clips.narration: Here are methane, ammonia, and water side by side, each with their central bond angle labeled: 109.5 degrees, 107 degrees, and 104.5 degrees. Notice the lone-pair clouds on ammonia and water are drawn larger than the bonding domains.

clips.changeMeaning: The overlay view is toggled on, superimposing all three molecules at their central atoms so students can directly see the bonding angle compress from 109.5 to 104.5 degrees as lone pairs are added.
clips.narration: Why are lone pairs bigger? A lone pair is held only by the central atom's nucleus, while a bonding pair is shared and pulled between two nuclei. With nothing pulling it toward a second atom, the lone pair spreads out and occupies more angular space, pushing the remaining bonding pairs closer together. This is why the H-X-H angle shrinks as more lone pairs are added.

modules.description: Presents a gallery of six real molecules spanning all five electron-domain geometries, each shown with its Lewis structure alongside its 3D structure for students to explore.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply VSEPR predictions to real molecules including CO2, BF3, CH4, PF5, SF6, NH3, H2O, and XeF4.
Name the electron-domain geometry, molecular geometry, and bond angles for each real molecule example.
instructions: Approach each molecule to see its Lewis structure and 3D structure side by side.
Confirm the count of bonding domains and lone pairs for each central atom.

clips.changeMeaning: The five all-bonding-domain example molecules spanning each electron-domain geometry are revealed together to form the main gallery display.
clips.narration: Welcome to the gallery of real molecules. Here you can see examples spanning all five electron-domain geometries: CO2, linear; BF3, trigonal planar; CH4, tetrahedral; PF5, trigonal bipyramidal; and SF6, octahedral. Approach each one to see its Lewis structure alongside its 3D shape.

clips.changeMeaning: The three lone-pair-modified example molecules are revealed to complete the gallery, letting students compare all eight named shapes across the five electron-domain geometry families.
clips.narration: Now here are three lone-pair-containing examples worth highlighting separately: ammonia, trigonal pyramidal; water, bent; and xenon tetrafluoride, square planar. Each comes from a tetrahedral or octahedral electron-domain geometry modified by one or more lone pairs. For each, count the bonding domains and lone pairs at the central atom to confirm the predicted shape.

modules.description: An interactive activity where students drag floating electron domains around a central atom into the correct minimum-repulsion geometry, progressing through domain counts and mixed bonding/lone-pair configurations.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Correctly position 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 electron domains into their minimum-repulsion arrangement.
Recognize that a lone pair occupies a standard electron-domain position even though it changes the resulting molecular geometry.
instructions: Drag each electron domain around the central atom until the full set snaps into the correct geometry.
Complete each round to advance to the next domain count.

components.text: Drag domains into a linear arrangement (2 domains)

clips.changeMeaning: Two draggable electron domains appear at arbitrary positions for the student to manipulate into the correct linear arrangement, beginning the interactive drag challenge.
clips.narration: Your turn. Drag these two electron domains around the central atom until they settle into the correct minimum-repulsion arrangement. Watch for the configuration to snap into place when you're close.

components.text: Drag domains into a trigonal planar arrangement (3 domains)

clips.changeMeaning: A third draggable domain is added and the instructional label updates, progressing the challenge from linear to trigonal planar arrangement practice.
clips.narration: Well done. Now let's try three domains: drag them into the trigonal planar arrangement, spaced 120 degrees apart.

components.text: Drag domains into a tetrahedral arrangement (4 domains, 1 lone pair shown in purple)

clips.changeMeaning: A fourth domain, colored as a lone pair, is added to introduce a mixed bonding/lone-pair configuration, testing whether students recognize the lone pair still occupies a standard tetrahedral electron-domain position.
clips.narration: Now for a mixed configuration: four domains total, but this time one of them is a lone pair, shown in purple. Drag all four into a tetrahedral arrangement. Notice that the lone pair takes a normal tetrahedral position even though the resulting molecular geometry, if you only look at the bonded atoms, would be trigonal pyramidal.

modules.description: An interactive activity where students view a Lewis structure of an unfamiliar molecule and select the matching 3D geometry from several candidates, with corrective feedback and reasoning after each choice.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Determine steric number and lone pair count from an unfamiliar Lewis structure.
Select the correct 3D molecular geometry matching a given Lewis structure, sampling across all five electron-domain geometries.
instructions: Determine the steric number and lone pair count.

components.text: SF4: count the domains around sulfur. What is the steric number?

clips.changeMeaning: The unfamiliar Lewis structure for SF4 and four candidate 3D structures are all revealed together, presenting the full multiple-choice prediction challenge to the student.
clips.narration: Here is the Lewis structure of SF4, sulfur tetrafluoride. Examine it: count the bonding domains and lone pairs on the central sulfur atom, determine the steric number, and then choose the 3D structure you think matches from the four candidates shown.

components.text: Correct! SF4: steric number 5, 1 lone pair → Seesaw

clips.changeMeaning: Candidate A (seesaw) is highlighted as correct in the feedback label after the student's selection, and the reasoning steps are recapped: count domains, find steric number, identify electron-domain geometry, account for lone pairs.
clips.narration: Let's check the reasoning. Sulfur has four bonds to fluorine and one lone pair, giving a steric number of five: trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry. With one lone pair occupying an equatorial position, the molecular geometry is seesaw. Candidate A is correct.

clips.changeMeaning: No new object changes; this clip narrates that the pick-the-structure challenge repeats with additional unfamiliar molecules beyond SF4, closing out this module's demonstrated round.
clips.narration: This challenge repeats with other unfamiliar molecules like ClF3, BrF5, and I3-, sampling all five electron-domain geometries. Each time, follow the same steps: count the domains, identify the electron-domain geometry, account for any lone pairs, and name the resulting molecular geometry.

modules.description: Closes the lab with a summary screen reviewing the five key concept areas covered: minimum-repulsion principle, the five electron-domain geometries, electron-domain vs molecular geometry, lone pair angular asymmetry, and application to real molecules.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recall and connect the five key concept areas of VSEPR theory covered in this lab.
instructions: Review the recap screen as each concept area is highlighted.

components.text:
1. Minimum Repulsion
2. Five Electron-Domain Geometries
3. Electron-Domain vs Molecular Geometry
4. Lone Pair Angular Asymmetry
5. Real Molecule Applications

clips.changeMeaning: The recap panel appears with concept 1, the minimum-repulsion principle, highlighted to begin the closing review sequence.
clips.narration: Let's recap what we've covered. First, the minimum-repulsion principle: electron domains around a central atom arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.

clips.changeMeaning: The recap panel color returns to its normal state, signaling the narration has moved through and summarized the remaining four concept areas to close the lab.
clips.narration: Second, the five electron-domain geometries: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral, each with its own characteristic domain count and angles. Third, the distinction between electron-domain geometry, which includes lone pairs, and molecular geometry, which describes only the positions of atoms. Fourth, lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, compressing bond angles below the idealized values. And fifth, we applied all of this to real molecules - water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, and XeF4 - and matched VSEPR predictions to observed structures.
